Order No.04/Dated: 12th March 2024 Ram Kisku and Dukhni Majhain have been acquitted and the judgment in TR Case No. 350 of 2009 convicting them under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code has been set-aside.
2. The prosecution case is that the respondents made demand of dowry and in connection therewith inflicted torture upon the victim lady in various ways.
In the trial altogether four witnesses were examined who supported the victim lady, who tendered evidence as CW4.
In TR Case No. 350 of 2009, the trial Judge referred to the evidence of defence witnesses and formed an opinion that they are not trustworthy witnesses.

In TR Case No.350 of 2009, the Judicial Magistrate 1 st Class,
Jamtara has held as under:
"11.
Defence has adduced the evidence of two witnesses.
DW1 is Devisher Tudu.
He states that a Santhal can marry twice and also separates customarily.
He further states that the complainant went away as a result of such separation after taking away two oxen.
He identifies the handwriting on a Panchayati Paper of 'chora-chori' as that of his nephew Ajit Tudu.
It is marked as 'Ext-A'.
In paragraph 4 he states that he had come to the court by chance and not for the purpose of giving evidence but agreed to do so when asked for it.
This shows that this witness is not speaking truth or atleast that he has not come with clean hands.
He admits that 'Ext-A' does not bear the signature/thumb impression of either the complainant or her father.
It also does not bear the date of preparation of the paper.
12.DW2 is Sahdeo Hembram.

He further states that a Santhal can marry seven times and even CW 2 and 3 have married twice.
In cross-examination he admits that he does not know as to who tore the leaf.
He further states that through the complainant was absent in the said meeting, her family members were present.
But 'Ext-A' does not bear the signature or thumb impression of any such member.

Thus this witness does not appear to be a trustworthy and his evidence cannot be relied upon.
13.In this case

, so far as charge u/s 498A IPC is concerned, CW 2, 3 and 4 have equivocally stated that the complainant was subjected to torture by accused no. 1 and 2 when their demand for a TV and motorcycle was not met by the father of the complainant.
Evidence regarding this has remain unshaken even in the cross-examination by the learned counsel for defence.
It is admitted fact that the remarriage took place after the complainant was driven out of her matrimonial home.
So accused no. 3 and 4 cannot be held liable for the torture given to the complainant during her stay at the matrimonial home.

No fact has come on record whether accused no. 3 and 4 knew previously that the accused no. 1 had a spouse living."
3.
The appellate Court has however rendered a decision that the prosecution witnesses made contradictory statements and there was no cogent evidence on demand of dowry.

In the Criminal Appeal No. 03 of 2009, the learned Sessions Judge held as under:
"13.

Considering that all the witnesses are interested witness and no independent witness has been examined by the prosecution the evidence of torture vague and omnibus, the evidence of "Panchayat"
admitted but paper has been suppressed by PW2, which has been produced by the defence and in support of said "Panchayat", 2 DWs have been examined, one belonging to the in-laws village of complainant and other belonging to the paternal village of the complainant, who have supported the holding of "Panchayat" in the year 2002, as well as that "Panchayat" ended in terms of verdict of chora-chori i.e. divorce between the accused and complainant from marital relationship, I hereby found that prosecution has not been able to prove the charges beyond shadow of all reasonable doubt but learned lower court has wrongly convicted the appellants by the impugned judgment and sentence, which is not sustainable in my view, therefore, the same is hereby set aside and appellants are acquitted from the charges giving benefit of serious doubt."
4.

Mr. Nityanand Pd. Choudhary, the learned counsel for the appellant submits that the judgment of acquittal delivered by the lower appellate Court ignores the fundamental rule that primacy has to be given to the judgment rendered by the trial Court.

sentences.text: This is by now well settled that the High Court while dealing with the judgment of acquittal shall keep in mind that the judgment of acquittal establishes the innocence of the accused and therefore only under the compelling circumstances the High Court shall interfere with the judgment of acquittal.

The judgment rendered by the lower appellate Court is founded on good reasons and on appreciation of the materials laid during the trial the lower appellate Court has held that the respondents are entitled for the benefit of doubt.
The lower appellate Court has recorded a finding that no evidence was laid as regards treatment of PW4 and the complaint of demand of dowry was vague.

The lower appellate Court has also referred to the defence witnesses and taking into consideration their evidence held that the judgment of conviction rendered in TR Case No. 350 of 2009 was unsustainable.
6.

Now in a situation like this, the High Court dealing with judgment of acquittal shall not enter into the realm of appreciation of evidence and shall not entertain the petition unless it is demonstrated that the judgment of acquittal shall amount to miscarriage of justice.

This is well settled a proposition in law that the prosecution has to establish its case beyond all reasonable doubts and wherever two views are possible the view leaning towards the accused shall be adopted by the Court [refer, "Harijana Thirupala v. Public Prosecutor" (2002) 6 SCC 470].
7.

In "Mrinal Das v. State of Tripura" (2011) 9 SCC 479 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as under:
"13.

entities.text: Mrinal Das v. State of Tripura" (2011) 9 SCC 479
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is clear that in an appeal against acquittal in the absence of perversity in the judgment and order, interference by this Court exercising its extraordinary jurisdiction, is not warranted.
However, if the appeal is heard by an appellate court, it being the final court of fact, is fully competent to reappreciate, reconsider and review the evidence and take its own decision.

In other words, the law does not prescribe any limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and the appellate court is free to arrive at its own conclusion keeping in mind that acquittal provides for presumption in favour of the accused.
The presumption of innocence is available to the person and in criminal jurisprudence every person is presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by the competent court.
If two reasonable views are possible on the basis of the evidence on record, the appellate court should not disturb the findings of acquittal."
4 Acquittal Appeal No. 16 of 2009 8. Having regard to the aforesaid facts and circumstances in the case, Acquittal Appeal No. 16 of 2009 is dismissed.
